title: Wonders of the Invisible World: Observations as Well Historical as Theological, upon the Nature, the Number, and the Operations of the Devils
author: Cotton Mather
publisher: Benjamin Harris, Boston; simultaneously Sam. Phillips, London (1693 being the date of the London edition; the Boston edition preceded it in 1692)
subject_focus: A defense of the Salem witch prosecution by Boston's leading Puritan minister, combining five trial accounts with demonological argument and covenant theology to justify the court's proceedings and the use of spectral evidence.
summary: Cotton Mather's Wonders of the Invisible World (1692) is the most important clerical defense of the Salem witch trials and a primary document in the history of spectral-evidence doctrine in New England. Written at the request of the Governor William Phips and the Salem court judges, it includes accounts of five Salem witch trials (George Burroughs, Bridget Bishop, Susanna Martin, Elizabeth How, Martha Carrier) interspersed with demonological essays arguing that New England was under special diabolic assault and that the court's proceedings were theologically justified. Mather argued that New England's covenanted status as God's chosen community made it a special target for satanic attack, and that the spectral evidence presented at the trials — testimony that the accused had appeared in spectral form to afflict the witnesses — was legally and theologically admissible as supporting evidence. The work drew immediate controversy from Robert Calef and Thomas Brattle, who contested both the evidential standards and Mather's account of specific trials.
scholarly_significance: Boyer and Nissenbaum in Salem Possessed (1974) situate Wonders of the Invisible World within the social and political dynamics of post-Salem Boston, analyzing how Mather's prosecution theology intersected with the clerical establishment's political interests. Norton in In the Devil's Snare (2002) provides the most historically sympathetic recent reading, situating Mather's fears within the genuine context of frontier trauma and King William's War rather than simply as credulity or political opportunism. Karlsen in The Devil in the Shape of a Woman (1987) uses Wonders as primary evidence for the gendered theology of witchcraft in Puritan New England. Clark in Thinking with Demons analyzes Mather as a representative of the late Puritan demonological tradition, situating his covenant-theology framework within the broader history of providential demonology. The work is indispensable as a primary source for the covenant-theology-prosecution-framework and spectral-evidence concept entries.

key_arguments.claim: New England's special status as God's covenanted community made it a primary target for diabolical assault; the Salem prosecutions were part of the larger spiritual war that the devil had declared against the Puritan experiment.

Spectral testimony — the afflicted testifying that the accused appeared in spectral form to torment them — was admissible and probative evidence of witchcraft, provided it was not the sole basis for conviction; Mather accepted the presumptive weight of spectral evidence while nominally acknowledging the possibility of the devil impersonating the innocent.

key_arguments.concept: The five trial accounts as exemplary cases
key_arguments.claim: Mather's detailed accounts of five trials provided the most complete narrative record of the Salem proceedings from the prosecution perspective and became major sources — albeit disputed ones — for subsequent historians of Salem.

relation_to_database: Wonders of the Invisible World is the primary prosecution defense document cited in the spectral-evidence and covenant-theology-prosecution-framework concept entries. The mather-cotton-b1663 scholar entry covers Mather's intellectual biography. Robert Calef's More Wonders of the Invisible World (1700) was written in direct response to this text.
scholarly_disagreement: Boyer and Nissenbaum find Mather's prosecution defense politically as well as theologically motivated, entangled with his father's political position and the clerical establishment's authority. Norton's more sympathetic reading argues that Mather's genuine fear of diabolic assault on New England reflected real trauma from the frontier wars and should not be reduced to political calculation. Calef's contemporary critique — that Mather misrepresented some trial records and that his spectral evidence doctrine was unsound — is sustained by some later historians and contested by others.
source_method: Published primary source; original Boston edition Benjamin Harris 1692; London edition 1693; reprinted in George Lincoln Burr, ed., Narratives of the Witchcraft Cases 1648-1706 (New York 1914)
